svg.aria-label: An annotated AWS CloudTrail StopLogging event showing the eventName, eventSource, userIdentity type and arn, sourceIPAddress, userAgent, errorCode, and requestParameters fields, each labelled with why it matters to an analyst
svg.title: Anatomy of a CloudTrail event — StopLogging
svg.text: READING A CLOUDTRAIL EVENT — StopLogging
eventName
The specific API call. StopLogging disables the audit trail — treat with ransomware-tier urgency.
eventSource
Which service handled the call. cloudtrail.amazonaws.com means this is an action on logging itself.
userIdentity.type / arn
Who made the call and their exact identity. A service account acting outside its normal job is the anomaly, not the plain name.
sourceIPAddress
Where the call originated — compare against this identity's known, historical source IPs.
userAgent — the tool that made the call (CLI, SDK, console). A sudden CLI call from an identity that always used the console is a shift worth noting.
errorCode — null means the call succeeded. A denied StopLogging (AccessDenied) is a very different, lower-urgency story than a successful one.
requestParameters
Exactly what was asked for — here, which trail was stopped. On other events this is what tells you the specific bucket, key, or
policy touched, turning "someone called an S3 API" into "someone changed this bucket's public access policy."
WHY THIS EVENT MATTERS
svc-report-gen is a service account — its normal job is generating reports, not managing CloudTrail. Two minutes earlier this
same identity called GetCallerIdentity (an orientation call an attacker makes right after gaining access). The account, action, and
timing together — not any single field — are what turn a technically-successful API call into an active-intrusion signal.
An attacker only disables logging when they are about to do something they do not want recorded.
Investigation pattern: pull every event for this userIdentity/accessKeyId, order by eventTime, and read it as a narrative —
auth, then recon (List*/Describe*/GetCallerIdentity), then escalation, then impact — the same way you would read a process tree.
